claims.text: High-entropy alloys can exhibit high mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Controlled addition of lightweight elements such as Al or Ti can reduce density while enabling high mechanical and environmental performance.
Al or Ti addition triggers solid-solution strengthening.
Al or Ti addition promotes in-situ formation of dense protective Al2O3 or TiO2 layers.
Protective oxide layers produced by lightweight-element addition improve corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The proposed lightweight-element additions and oxide layers enhance mechanical strength.
Exceeding an optimal lightweight-element concentration causes phase instability or deleterious transformations that impair performance.
A near-equiatomic CoCrFeNi-based baseline HEA can be treated as a single-phase alloy.
Lightweight-element addition produces a fine-grained microstructure.
Atomic-size mismatch introduced by lightweight elements enhances solid-solution strengthening.
A dense, adherent oxide scale acts as a physical barrier that slows oxidation and corrosive attack.
The protective oxide scale maintains mechanical strength at high temperature.
Excess lightweight elements can produce phase separation or brittle intermetallic phases.
An optimal lightweight-element addition will reduce density relative to the baseline alloy.
An optimal lightweight-element addition will increase yield strength and hardness relative to the baseline alloy.
An optimal lightweight-element addition will lower corrosion current density in 3.5% NaCl relative to the baseline alloy.
An optimal lightweight-element addition will reduce oxidation rate and oxide weight gain near 900°C relative to the baseline alloy.
Above a critical lightweight-element concentration, mechanical integrity, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance deteriorate.
The optimal concentration range depends on the lightweight element and the alloy's other constituents.
